claim: Grid cells in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) encode position using a distributed representation across multiple neural populations (modules), each possessing a distinct spatial scale.
source: Grid cells in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) encode position using a distributed representation across multiple neural populations (modules), each possessing a distinct spatial scale.
evidence: This is a well-established finding in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The modular structure of the grid cell representation confers the neural code with large capacity.
source: The modular structure of the representation confers the grid cell neural code with large capacity.
evidence: This claim is supported by theoretical work cited in the manuscript and is a central premise of the study.

claim: Small incompatible drifts in different modules, driven by noise, can rapidly lead to large, abrupt shifts in the represented position, resulting in catastrophic readout errors.
source: Small incompatible drifts in different modules, driven by noise, can rapidly lead to large, abrupt shifts in the represented position, resulting in catastrophic readout errors.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations and theoretical analysis in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 1A.

claim: The proposed coupling mechanism suppresses incompatible drifts between modules, allowing for a stable embedding of a two-dimensional variable (position) in a higher dimensional neural attractor.
source: The coupling suppresses incompatible drifts, allowing for a stable embedding of a two-dimensional variable (position) in a higher dimensional neural attractor, while preserving the large capacity.
evidence: This is the main theoretical result of the paper, demonstrated through mathematical analysis and simulations.

claim: The coupling mechanism may be implemented by recurrent synaptic connectivity within the MEC with a relatively simple and biologically plausible structure.
source: We propose that coupling of this type may be implemented by recurrent synaptic connectivity within the MEC with a relatively simple and biologically plausible structure.
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal based on the model architecture described in the manuscript.

claim: Grid cells in the MEC have been linked to an animal's estimate of its position within its environment.
source: A notable exception is the hippocampal formation, where neural activity has been linked to high level cognitive variables such as an animal's estimate of its position within its environment (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; Moser et al., 2008; Taube et al., 1990), or its estimate of elapsed time within a trial of a trained behavioral task (Manns et al., 2007; Pastalkova et al., 2008; Itskov et al., 2011; Eichenbaum, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental work.

claim: Grid cells were discovered in the medial entorhinal cortex.
source: Specifically, the representation of position by grid cells (Hafting et al., 2005) in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) has led to new, unexpected insights on the neural coding of such quantities
evidence: This is a well-known discovery in neuroscience, cited in the manuscript.

claim: Grid cells are organized into modules with distinct spatial scales.
source: even though position is a low dimensional variable, it is jointly encoded by several distinct populations of cells (modules: Stensola et al., 2012), exhibiting periodic spatial responses with varying spatial scales.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations cited in the manuscript.

claim: All grid cells within a module are characterized by the same grid spacing and orientation, differing only by a rigid translation.
source: The spatial responses of all grid cells within a module are characterized by the same grid spacing and orientation, while differing from each other only by a rigid translation.
evidence: This is an established property of grid cells within modules, supported by experimental data.

claim: The representation of position by each module is ambiguous, but the joint activity in several modules constitutes a highly efficient and unambiguous neural code.
source: The representation of position by each module is ambiguous, but taken together, the joint activity in several modules constitutes a highly efficient and unambiguous neural code (see Burak, 2014).
evidence: This is a theoretical result supported by citations.

claim: The grid cell code possesses a high dynamic range that greatly exceeds the performance of unimodal coding schemes such as place cells in the hippocampus.
source: Due to its distributed organization, the grid cell code possesses a high dynamic range (ratio between the range of unambiguous representation and resolution; Burak, 2014), greatly exceeding the performance of unimodal coding schemes such as the representation of position by place cells in the hippocampus (Fiete et al., 2008; Sreenivasan and Fiete, 2011; Mathis et al., 2012b; Wei et al., 2015; Mosheiff et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by theoretical analyses cited in the manuscript.

claim: Neurons within a module maintain strict relationships in their joint activity.
source: Neurons within a module maintain strict relationships in their joint activity (Yoon et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: The relationships between neurons within a module are maintained across environments.
source: These relationships are maintained across environments (Fyhn et al., 2007); under abrupt distortions of the environment (Barry et al., 2007; Yoon et al., 2013); in novel environments (Barry et al., 2012; Yoon et al., 2013), in which stable place fields are absent; during hippocampal inactivation (Almog et al., 2019); under genetic perturbations that disrupt the spatial periodicity in the response of individual cells (Allen et al., 2014); and in sleep (Trettel et al., 2019; Gardner et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental studies cited.

claim: The rigidity of the correlation structure suggests that neural activity within a module is tightly coordinated by recurrent connectivity, consistent with attractor models of grid cell activity.
source: The rigidity of the correlation structure strongly suggests that the neural activity within a module is tightly coordinated by recurrent connectivity, consistent with attractor models of grid cell activity (McNaughton et al., 2006; Fuhs and Touretzky, 2006; Guanella et al., 2007; Burak and Fiete, 2009), which propose that synaptic connectivity restricts the joint activity within a module to lie on a two-dimensional manifold.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations and theoretical models.

claim: Attractor models propose that synaptic connectivity restricts the joint activity within a module to lie on a two-dimensional manifold.
source: consistent with attractor models of grid cell activity (McNaughton et al., 2006; Fuhs and Touretzky, 2006; Guanella et al., 2007; Burak and Fiete, 2009), which propose that synaptic connectivity restricts the joint activity within a module to lie on a two-dimensional manifold.
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal from cited models.

claim: Calcium imaging studies in rats running on a virtual one-dimensional track revealed a relationship between position on the cortical sheet and the preferred firing locations of grid cells, as predicted by attractor models.
source: Additional support for attractor models has been recently obtained by imaging activity of multiple grid cells using calcium imaging in rats running on a virtual one-dimensional track (Heys et al., 2014; Gu et al., 2018). These studies revealed a relationship between position on the cortical sheet and the preferred firing locations of grid cells, as predicted by the variants of attractor models that rely on distance-dependent connectivity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental studies using calcium imaging.

claim: The maintenance of a coherent representation of position across modules necessitates some form of coupling between them.
source: Considering that noise may corrupt the representation of position in each module separately, the maintenance of a coherent representation of position across modules necessitates some form of coupling between them (Welinder et al., 2008; Sreenivasan and Fiete, 2011; Burak, 2014).
evidence: This is a theoretical argument supported by citations.

claim: Incoherent drifts in the positions represented by different modules can rapidly produce a joint representation of position that is incompatible with any position in the close vicinity of the animal.
source: Figure 1A demonstrates the need for this coupling: incoherent drifts in the positions represented by different modules, accrued due to noise, can rapidly produce a joint representation of position that is incompatible with any position in the close vicinity of the animal (Fiete et al., 2008; Welinder et al., 2008; Burak, 2014; Vágó and Ujfalussy, 2018).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1A and supported by theoretical work.

claim: The coupling should restrict changes in the states of different modules to lie within the two-dimensional sub-space that corresponds to smooth movement of the animal within its local environment.
source: The desired coupling across modules is more subtle than the one observed within a module: the coupling should restrict changes in the states of different modules to lie within the two-dimensional sub-space that corresponds to smooth movement of the animal within its local environment.
evidence: This is a design requirement for the coupling mechanism proposed in the paper.

claim: To preserve the high dynamic range of the code, the coupling should not restrict the dimensionality of the accessible steady states.
source: However, to preserve the high dynamic range of the code, the coupling should not restrict the dimensionality of the accessible steady states.
evidence: This is a design requirement for the coupling mechanism.

claim: The double-ring architecture includes a mechanism for updates based on velocity inputs and was proposed as a model for integration of angular velocity inputs by head direction cells in rodents.
source: More specifically, we consider the double-ring architecture (Xie et al., 2002), which includes a mechanism for updates based on velocity inputs, and was proposed as a model for integration of angular velocity inputs by head direction cells in rodents.
evidence: This is a description of an existing model from the literature.

claim: Recent discoveries in the Drosophila melanogaster central complex point to a representation of heading that is maintained by neural circuitry with close similarity to the double-ring architecture.
source: Recent discoveries in the Drosophila melanogaster central complex point to a representation of heading that is maintained by neural circuitry with close similarity to this architecture (Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015; Turner-Evans et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2017; Green et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by experimental studies in Drosophila.

claim: The coupling can be implemented by recurrent connectivity within the MEC, between modules and within a single module.
source: Thus, the coupling can be implemented by recurrent connectivity within the MEC, between modules and within a single module.
evidence: This follows from the mathematical structure of the coupling mechanism.

claim: The synaptic connectivity between any two coupled modules is all-to-all in the sense that every neuron in one module is connected to every neuron in the other module, with synaptic weights whose magnitudes are uniform.
source: The resulting synaptic connectivity between any two coupled modules is all-to-all in the sense that every neuron in one module is connected to every neuron in the other module, with synaptic weights whose magnitudes are uniform (see Materials and methods, Equation 12).
evidence: This is a property of the proposed connectivity structure.

claim: The sign of each synaptic weight depends only on the sub-population (left or right) of the pre- and post-synaptic neurons.
source: The sign of each synaptic weight depends only on the sub-population (left or right) of the pre- and post-synaptic neurons.
evidence: This is a property of the proposed connectivity structure.

claim: The connectivity is completely symmetric to rotation in the two modules, thus preserving the ability to obtain a combinatorially large manifold of steady states.
source: This connectivity is completely symmetric to rotation in the two modules, thus preserving the ability to obtain a combinatorially large manifold of steady states in which activity bumps can be placed in any combination of positions.
evidence: This is a consequence of the symmetry in the connectivity structure.

claim: Under the coupling conditions, the two coupled modules shift in a coordinated manner, even if they receive incompatible velocity inputs.
source: Hence, under these conditions, the two coupled modules shift in a coordinated manner, even if they receive incompatible velocity inputs.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the simulations shown in Figure 3.

claim: The coupling substantially reduces the mismatch accrued between the trajectories of the different modules, compared to the uncoupled case.
source: The coupling substantially reduces the mismatch accrued between the trajectories of the different modules, compared to the uncoupled case, Figure 4F.
evidence: This is shown quantitatively in Figure 4F.

claim: The lack of deviations between the phase trajectories in the coupled case is an essential difference between the dynamics of the coupled and uncoupled modules.
source: The lack of deviations between the phase trajectories, seen in the coupled case (Figure 4E–F), is an essential difference between the dynamics of the coupled and uncoupled modules.
evidence: This is observed in the simulation results.

claim: The coupling of modules stabilizes the grid cell code and prevents catastrophic errors caused by uncoupled drift in the phases of different modules.
source: We next aim to validate our hypothesis that the coupling of modules stabilizes the grid cell code, and more specifically, prevents catastrophic errors that can be caused by uncoupled drift in the phases of different modules (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is validated through simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: In the case of coupled modules, the decoded trajectory is similar to the input, but gradually accrues an error relative to the true trajectory due to noise in the inputs.
source: In the case of coupled modules the decoded trajectory is similar to the input (Figure 5A), but due to the noise in the inputs, it gradually accrues an error relative to the true trajectory.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Without coupling, the position read out from the network activity diverges sharply from the true trajectory and is often discontinuous in time.
source: Without coupling, the position read out from the network activity diverges sharply from the true trajectory (Figure 5B). Moreover, the readout trajectory is often discontinuous in time, and thus cannot be a good approximation to any reasonable path of the animal.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5B.

claim: The discontinuity in readout arises from uncorrelated drifts of the modules which, combined with the periodic nature of the grid pattern, cause catastrophic readout errors.
source: The discontinuity arises from uncorrelated drifts of the modules which, combined with the periodic nature of the grid pattern, cause catastrophic readout errors, much larger than the errors accrued in the phases of each module separately (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is explained theoretically and demonstrated in simulations.

claim: In all realizations with coupling, the readout is coordinated with the input trajectory.
source: In all realizations with coupling, the readout is coordinated with the input trajectory (Figure 5C, blue).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C based on 100 simulations.

claim: Without coupling, almost all realizations exhibit discontinuities within a time interval of 20s.
source: In contrast, without coupling almost all realizations exhibit discontinuities within a time interval of 20s (Figure 5C, red).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C based on 100 simulations.

claim: The MSE grows sharply in the uncoupled system a few seconds after the start of the simulation, coinciding with the first appearance of discontinuities in the decoded position.
source: However, a few seconds after the start of the simulation, the MSE grows sharply in the uncoupled system (dashed line in Figure 5D). The time at which this starts to happen coincides with the first appearance of discontinuities in the decoded position (compare Figure 5 panels C and D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The dramatic reduction achieved by the coupling between modules arises primarily from the elimination of catastrophic readout errors.
source: Thus, the dramatic reduction achieved by the coupling between modules arises primarily from the elimination of catastrophic readout errors.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the analysis of the simulation results.

claim: The simple readout of velocity used to couple the modules is a good approximation for the phase velocity driven by intrinsic neural noise.
source: In Appendix A.2 we show that the simple readout of velocity used to couple the modules (Equation 4), is a good approximation for the phase velocity driven by intrinsic neural noise, suggesting that the coupling introduced previously can help suppress uncoordinated drifts.
evidence: This is shown mathematically in Appendix A.2.

claim: When the modules are coupled, the diffusion of the two modules is highly anisotropic, with the first principal axis closely matching the direction of coordinated motion.
source: When the modules are coupled, with the same coupling strengths as in Figure 3, the diffusion of the two modules is highly anisotropic (Figure 6A). The first principal axis of the diffusion tensor (red ellipse in Figure 6A) closely matches the direction of coordinated motion (dashed line in Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A through calculation of the diffusion tensor.

claim: Discontinuities in the decoded trajectory occur both in the uncoupled and coupled networks with Poisson neurons, but they are much more rare in the coupled network.
source: Discontinuities in the decoded trajectory occur both in the uncoupled and coupled networks, but they are much more rare in the coupled network (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B for networks with intrinsic neural noise.

claim: The readout MSE is reduced dramatically in the coupled network with intrinsic neural noise.
source: Accordingly, the readout MSE is reduced dramatically in the coupled network (Figure 6C, note the logarithmic scale).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The coupling is effective not only in stabilizing the neural representation in response to noisy inputs, but also with respect to internal stochasticity within the grid cell network.
source: Thus, the coupling is effective not only in stabilizing the neural representation in response to noisy inputs, but also with respect to internal stochasticity within the grid cell network.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations with Poisson spiking neurons.

claim: The number of grid cell modules in the entorhinal cortices of rats and mice is unknown, but there is direct evidence for the existence of four modules.
source: The number of grid cell modules in the entorhinal cortices of rats and mice is unknown. So far there is direct evidence for the existence of four modules, but the number may be larger (Stensola et al., 2012; Rowland et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations cited in the manuscript.

claim: Increasing the number of modules reduces the rate of readout discontinuities within the range of a given environment, but offers the possibility to unambiguously represent larger environments.
source: increasing the number of modules reduces the rate of readout discontinuities within the range of a given environment, but it offers the possibility to unambiguously represent larger environments (Fiete et al., 2008; Mathis et al., 2012a; Wei et al., 2015; Vágó and Ujfalussy, 2018), for which the error rate is higher Figure 5—figure supplement 2E–J.
evidence: This is supported by theoretical work and demonstrated in supplementary figures.

claim: The proposed velocity coupling mechanism may play an especially important role in generating a cognitive map of a novel environment.
source: Thus, the velocity coupling mechanism proposed in this work may play an especially important role in generating a cognitive map of a novel environment.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the limitations of hippocampal coupling in novel environments.

claim: Phase resets occur in the grid cell representation upon encounters with environmental boundaries.
source: Experimentally, it has been demonstrated that phase resets occur in the grid cell representation upon encounters with enviornmental boundaries (Hardcastle et al., 2015; Keinath et al., 2018; Ocko et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by experimental studies.

claim: Phase resets can be implemented in attractor models of grid cells by inputs to grid cells from border cells.
source: and it has been argued theoretically that such resets can be implemented in attractor models of grid cells by inputs to grid cells from border cells (Hardcastle et al., 2015; Keinath et al., 2018; Ocko et al., 2018; Pollock et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal from cited work.

claim: The synaptic connectivity proposed by Kang and Balasubramanian (2019) is spatially local and tends to produce interlocked patterns of activity in adjacent modules with shared spatial periodicity.
source: In contrast, the synaptic connectivity considered in Kang and Balasubramanian (2019) is spatially local. Consequently, it tends to produce interlocked patterns of activity in adjacent modules, with shared spatial periodicity, and preferred relative spatial phases.
evidence: This is a comparison with another model from the literature.

claim: The connectivity considered in this work is all-to-all and designed to be invariant to any static, relative shift in the module phases, so all combinations of phases are steady states.
source: An important difference between the network architecture explored in Kang and Balasubramanian (2019) and the architecture explored here, is that we consider connectivity between modules which is all-to-all (every grid cell in one module projects to every grid cell in the other module), and is designed to be invariant to any static, relative shift in the module phases. Hence, all combinations of phases are steady states of the dynamics.
evidence: This is a description of the proposed architecture.

claim: Using negative self-coupling of velocities, it is possible to suppress fluctuations to substantially reduce noise-driven diffusion and stabilize the represented memory in a single ring attractor.
source: Using the negative self-coupling of velocities, introduced in this work, it is possible to suppress these fluctuations to substantially reduce the noise-driven diffusion and stabilize the represented memory.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the proposed mechanism.

claim: The velocity coupling mechanism may be relevant to the stabilization of short-term memory in head direction cells of rodents and insects.
source: Thus, the velocity coupling mechanism identified in this work may be relevant to the stabilization of short-term memory in head directions cells of rodents (Taube, 2007) and insects (Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015), where there is no evidence for slowly decaying deformations in the shape of the activity bump.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential applications of the mechanism.

claim: If one module is disconnected from the others, the disconnected module is expected to weaken its response to velocity inputs and increase its grid spacing.
source: An interesting prediction arises under a scenario in which one of the modules is disconnected from the others. This removes positive couplings from the other modules, but leaves the negative self coupling within the module intact. Hence, the disconnected module is expected to weaken its response to velocity inputs, and increase its grid spacing.
evidence: This is a testable prediction, illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The existence of a coupling mechanism must be tested under conditions in which external sensory cues are weak.
source: The existence of a coupling mechanism must therefore be tested under conditions in which external sensory cues are weak (Burak, 2014).
evidence: This is a methodological recommendation for experimental testing.

claim: During sleep, weak correlations between grid cells from different modules are significantly reduced.
source: During sleep, these weak correlations are significantly reduced (Trettel et al., 2019; Gardner et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: To test for the existence of a velocity coupling mechanism, it is desirable to test for correlations in the updates of phases of different modules, rather than directly testing for correlations in their phases.
source: In order to test for the existence of a velocity coupling mechanism, it is desirable to test for correlations in the updates of phases of different modules, instead of directly testing for correlations in their phases.
evidence: This is a methodological recommendation for experimental testing.

claim: Conjunctive cells observed mostly in layer III and deeper layers of the MEC may provide the substrate for the connectivity proposed in the model.
source: A specific population of cells that may provide the substrate for the connectivity proposed in our model are the conjunctive cells observed mostly in layer III and deeper layers of the MEC (Sargolini et al., 2006), which play a pivotal role in models of path integration in the grid cell system.
evidence: This is a speculation about the biological implementation of the model.

claim: Recent evidence hints that synaptic connections between excitatory cells in the MEC may be more limited in range, but of sufficient spatial extent to allow for coupling of adjacent modules.
source: Recent evidence (Fu et al., 2018) hints that synaptic connections between excitatory cells in the MEC may be more limited in range, but of sufficient spatial extent to allow for coupling of adjacent modules.
evidence: This is based on recent experimental findings.
